trap: Becomes generic self-denial moralism ("give something up") detached from the specific refusal it answers — Peter's, and ours, of a suffering Messiah — or a martyr-glorification that skips past how sharp and immediate the correction is.
hinge: Love for Jesus is exactly what makes Peter say the wrong thing — Jerome will not even call it a devil's suggestion, only misdirected affection — yet Jesus names it "Satan" all the same, because a Christ without a cross is a temptation no matter who offers it.

doors.landing: The love that gets it backwards
doors.claim: Peter's rebuke comes from real affection, not malice, and is corrected all the harder for it — the shape of love has to be re-taught, not just the fact of it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: This error of the Apostle, proceeding from the warmth of his affection, will never seem to me a suggestion of the devil.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Peter had said, 'Be it far from thee, Lord; this shall not be unto thee'; and had been answered, 'Get thee behind me, Satan'; but the Lord was not satisfied with this rebuke alone.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Our Lord is not recorded to have given so sharp a reproof to any other of his apostles on any occasion. He saw it was needful for the pride of Peter's heart, puffed up with the commendation lately given him.

doors.say: Peter said what he said because he loved Jesus — and love was exactly what needed correcting, not condemning.
doors.do: Have them name one way their love for someone has led them to want to spare them a necessary hard road, and sit with the discomfort of letting go.

doors.landing: Deny yourself, not just your stuff
doors.claim: Self-denial is not asceticism about possessions but ceasing to be who you were, in order to become what you are not yet.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: He denies himself whosoever is changed for the better, and begins to be what he was not, and ceases to be what he was.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: We are to follow our Lord by taking up the cross of His passion; and if not in deed, yet in will, bear Him company.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Let him in all things deny his own will, however pleasing, and do the will of God, however painful.

doors.say: Denying yourself isn't giving something up for Lent — it's ceasing to be the person you've been.
doors.do: Ask them to name one way of being — not one habit — that following Jesus requires them to stop being.

doors.landing: No exchange rate for a soul
doors.claim: The arithmetic of self-preservation never balances — nothing in the whole world can be traded back for the life spent saving it wrongly.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: If you should reign over the whole world, you would not be able to buy your soul.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: He gains the world who does not deny himself... and thence suffers the loss of his soul.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Let neither gains, nor fear, nor anything else draw a man back from salvation: because a man will be able to give nothing earthly for a soul that is lost.

doors.say: There is no amount of the world you could buy back your soul with, once you've spent it protecting the wrong thing.
doors.do: Have them name one thing they're currently spending their life to protect, and ask whether it's worth the trade.

doors.claim: Jeremiah's lament is in the Bible, not edited out: a faithful life can be lonely and painful, and saying so is not unbelief.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: His whole prophetical life had been to him a time of mourning and solitude, a time when he sat alone, mourning and weeping in secret for the wrath of God revealed to him against his people.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Jeremiah, though a great prophet, was (as Elijah) a man subject to like passions with other men.

doors.say: Jeremiah told God the truth about how much it hurt. God didn't strike him down for it. God answered.
doors.do: Give them permission to bring their honest complaint to God this week, out loud, without dressing it up.

doors.landing: Return, and be as my mouth
doors.claim: God's reply to the complaint is a call back: turn from distrust, sort the precious from the worthless, and speak for God again.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: These are God's words to the prophet, rebuking his distrust in God, and promising him, that if he did return from his distrust in God's providence, he would restore him to the former favour he had with him.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Let us consider how great a reward the discourse of a teacher has, if it shall have willed to deliver from error any man, and to call him back from the number of those that sin.

doors.say: God didn't tell Jeremiah to quit. God said: come back, and I will put my words in your mouth again.
doors.do: Ask them to name the word of truth they have stopped speaking because it cost too much, and to speak it once this week.

complementary.gravity: Jeremiah, who once ate God's words with joy, now sits alone in pain and asks whether God has become a failing brook; God answers not with comfort but with a call to return, to separate the precious from the vile, and so be "as my mouth" (Jeremiah 15). The Psalm asks God to try the heart; Paul says overcome evil with good (Romans 12); and Jesus rebukes Peter and names the cross as the road. The nerve: faithfulness that hurts, and a God who answers our complaint by calling us back to the work.

synthesis.convergence: Jeremiah's calling has left him alone and aching, and when he complains God calls him to turn back and speak the precious rather than the vile (Jeremiah 15); the psalmist invites God to test his heart (Psalm 26); Paul asks for a love that blesses persecutors and overcomes evil with good (Romans 12); and Jesus tells Peter the way to life runs through the cross (Matthew 16). Each reading refuses the painless version of faithfulness, and meets suffering with a renewed call rather than an exit.
synthesis.claim: Faithfulness sometimes hurts, and God's answer to our honest complaint is not escape but a call to return and keep speaking.
synthesis.here: For people worn thin by doing right at a cost — caregivers, truth-tellers, those holding unpopular convictions — the move is to let them complain as Jeremiah did, and then to hear God's "return" as renewal rather than rebuke.

semicontinuous.gravity: Moses meets God at a bush that burns without being consumed and is sent, reluctant, toward a suffering people (Exodus 3); Paul's catalog of love in Romans 12 crests in "overcome evil with good"; and Jesus — immediately after being named the Christ — announces he must suffer and die, and is rebuked by the very man who just confessed him. The nerve: the same confession that names Jesus rightly can, in the very next breath, refuse the shape his mission actually takes.

synthesis.convergence: Moses is sent by a God who has "surely seen the affliction of my people" yet sends him toward more suffering, not around it (Exodus 3); Paul's love-ethic peaks in "overcome evil with good," itself a cross-shaped command (Romans 12); and Jesus names the cross the same day Peter names him Christ. Every reading refuses a rescue that bypasses suffering — deliverance always goes through it.
synthesis.claim: You cannot love Jesus rightly and skip the cross — not his, and eventually not your own.
synthesis.here: For people who want Jesus as comfort without cost, don't soften 'take up your cross' — sharpen it the way Jesus did with Peter: the correction is loving precisely because it isn't gentle.

subtract: Three landings — the miscorrected love, the reshaped self-denial, or the impossible exchange. Choose one and let the others go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
